page.title: Virtual summit producer guide for buyers
page.description: Learn what a virtual summit producer delivers, how to pick platform and production, timelines, staffing, workstreams and replay follow‑up.
page.h1: What should you decide first about a virtual summit producer?
page.definition: A virtual summit producer is a service that plans, runs and records multi‑session online events, handling run‑of‑show, speaker rehearsals, live moderation, backup streaming and post‑event editing. It also coordinates registration, engagement tools, recording delivery and follow‑up reporting for sponsors and attendees.
page.quick_answer: Start by defining the event scope, audience size and required deliverables, then match those needs to a platform and a production crew that can own the run of show and backup stream. West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations.

sections.h2: What does a virtual summit producer actually deliver?

blocks.p: The producer builds the run of show, prepares speaker briefs, runs rehearsals, creates branded slide templates and lower thirds, operates the live stream, moderates Q&A, maintains a backup stream, and delivers edited recordings plus highlight clips for reuse across marketing channels. They also coordinate registration integration, engagement tools such as polls and chat, and post‑event reporting dashboards.

ul: Run of show and speaker briefs
Rehearsal sessions on the live platform
Branded slide templates and lower thirds

sections.h2: How do I choose the right platform and production model?

blocks.p: Choose a platform that matches your licence model: per‑host licences sized by capacity suit large enterprise webinars, self‑serve monthly plans work for recurring webinars run by an internal team, and annual contracts quoted by sales fit multi‑day summits and hybrid events that require dedicated support and custom branding.

sections.h2: What timeline and staffing do I need for a summit versus a webinar?

blocks.p: A summit typically needs six to eight weeks of planning with a show caller, speaker manager, moderator and platform operator, while a webinar can be ready in three to four weeks with a single producer who handles scheduling, rehearsal and live switching. The longer lead time allows venue AV lock, speaker travel coordination and multiple rehearsal cycles.

ol: Lock venue AV and platform contracts
Run full rehearsal two to five days before
Go live with show caller and backup stream

sections.h2: Which workstreams and owners should I assign?

blocks.p: Eight workstreams each need a single owner to avoid gaps in registration, agenda, speaker management, production, streaming, engagement, recording and follow‑up; assigning clear accountability reduces last‑minute scrambling and ensures each deliverable has a sign‑off gate. A shared project board in Asana or Monday.com keeps owners aligned on dates and dependencies.

sections.h2: How do I handle recordings, replays and follow‑up?

blocks.p: Send the replay within twenty four to forty eight hours, provide edited clips for social channels, and feed attendance data into your CRM for nurture sequences; timely delivery keeps the conversation alive while the content is fresh. Include a short survey link to capture feedback and segment leads for targeted follow‑up campaigns.

ul: Enroll engaged leads in nurture flow

faq.q: What is the typical cost range for a produced virtual summit?
faq.a: A full‑service summit usually falls between ten thousand and fifty thousand dollars, depending on session count, hybrid elements and crew size; a moderated webinar starts around two thousand five hundred dollars. Pricing varies with platform choice, speaker travel and custom branding.

faq.q: How many rehearsals are recommended before going live?
faq.a: Schedule one full rehearsal on the actual platform two to five days before the event and a technical check sixty minutes before start to catch audio, video and backup stream issues. This reduces surprise failures and gives speakers confidence for the live audience.

faq.q: Who should own the run of show during a multi‑session summit?
faq.a: Assign a dedicated show caller who controls timing, cues speakers, manages the backup stream and coordinates with the platform operator; this role is separate from moderation and speaker management. Clear ownership prevents gaps when sessions run long or technical issues arise.

faq.q: What follow‑up actions turn attendees into owned audience?
faq.a: Export registration data to your CRM, tag attendees by session interest, send a personalized replay email within two days, and invite them to a community space or newsletter for ongoing engagement. Track open rates and click‑throughs to refine future nurture sequences.
